extraction_notes.note: The two main-text proof outlines (Sec. 4.2.1 and 4.3) are proof sketches; per the 'A proof sketch' rule they carry rigor: semi_formal and alternative proves edges, although the finishing step warns that rigor does not belong on proofs. Kept as the rule states.

The full proofs of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 have no proof environment: the proof of Thm 4.1 is taken as the text of Appendix D before subsection D.1, and the proof of Thm 4.2 as subsection E.2 (Steps One-Six); the supporting propositions/lemmas in the other subsections keep their own nodes and proofs.

Appendix A constructs a circle-valued distribution and verifies both Fourier assumptions with eta = k; kept as one example (illustrating Assumptions A.1/A.2) rather than a claim plus prose proof, since no separate statement is made before the argument.
Appendix B ('Explicit Solutions of KIV-O') is a derivation of closed-form estimators; typed as an algorithm (closed-form KIV-O) rather than a claim.

Subsection D.1.1 argues an oracle inequality in prose before Proposition D.6; extracted as a claim (the final inequality) with a prose proof, and linked to the proof of Prop. D.6 which uses 'the inequality immediately preceding this proposition'.

Ubiquitous notation definitions (L^p spaces, operator norm, min/max, asymptotic inequalities, bracket notation, natural numbers) are kept as nodes without term edges, since they are used in nearly every node; the related-work discussion (Sec. 3, 3.1-3.2) and the conclusion are not extracted apart from one remark and one open problem.
The 'Roadmap for Proof of Theorem 4.1' consists of omitted diagrams of result dependencies; dependencies were taken from the \Cref references in the proofs instead.
Equations eq:f_lambda and eq:bar_f_lambda in Appendix C restate eq:f_lambda_main and eq:bar_f_lambda_main; recorded as also_stated_at of those equation nodes instead of separate nodes.

nodes.name: NPIV-O model
nodes.statement_short: Model $Y=f_*(X,O)+\epsilon$ with $\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid Z,O]=0$: nonparametric IV regression with observed covariates $O$.

nodes.name: NPIV-O structural equation (eq:npiv_o_intro)
nodes.statement: Y = f_{\ast}(X, O) + \epsilon, \quad \mathbb{E}[\epsilon \mid Z, O] = 0 .
nodes.label: eq:npiv_o_intro

nodes.name: Heterogeneous dose response curve
nodes.statement: We refer to $f_{\ast}$ as the \emph{heterogeneous dose response curve}, and it is our target of interest.

nodes.name: Exclusion restriction
nodes.statement: By Eq. \eqref{eq:npiv_o_intro}, we implicitly assume that $Z$ can only possibly affect $Y$ through $X$, a condition known as \emph{exclusion restriction}.

nodes.name: Instrumental relevance
nodes.statement: We also require that $Z$ and $X$ are not independent, a condition known as \emph{instrumental relevance}.

nodes.name: Valid instrumental variable
nodes.statement: A random variable $Z$ that satisfies these requirements is referred to as a valid instrumental variable.

nodes.name: Conditional moment restriction
nodes.statement_short: The NPIV-O model is equivalent to the conditional moment restriction $\mathbb{E}[Y|Z,O]=(Tf_*)(Z,O)$.
conclusions: Eq.~\eqref{eq:npiv_o_intro} is equivalent to the following \emph{conditional moment restriction} for $f_{\ast}$:

nodes.name: Inverse problem E[Y|Z,O]=(Tf*)(Z,O) (eq:inverse_problem)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z, O]=(Tf_\ast)(Z, O).
nodes.label: eq:inverse_problem

nodes.name: T is the identity on functions of O only
nodes.statement:
With the presence of $O$, $T$ acts as an identity operator on the infinite dimensional function space
\begin{align} \mathcal{F}_1 = \{f : f(X, O) = f_1(O), \text{ } f_1 \in L^2(P_{O})\} \subset L^2(P_{XO}),
\end{align}
rendering the operator non-compact.
nodes.statement_short: On the space $\mathcal{F}_1$ of functions of $O$ alone, $T$ is the identity, so $T$ is not compact.
assumptions: With the presence of $O$
conclusions: $T$ acts as an identity operator on the infinite dimensional function space
rendering the operator non-compact.

nodes.name: Function space F_1 of functions of O only (eq:calF_1_espace)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{F}_1 = \{f : f(X, O) = f_1(O), \text{ } f_1 \in L^2(P_{O})\} \subset L^2(P_{XO}),
nodes.label: eq:calF_1_espace

nodes.name: Function space F_2 (functions of X only)
nodes.statement: We consider another function space $\mathcal{F}_2 = \{f : f(X, O) = f_2(X), \;\; f_2 \in L^2(P_{X})\} \subset L^2(P_{XO})$.

nodes.name: Data-generating measure and domains
nodes.statement: Consider $P$ the joint data-generating probability measure over $(Z,O,X,Y)$, where $Z\in \mathcal{Z} := [0,1]^{d_z}$ denotes the instrument, $O \in \mathcal{O}:=[0,1]^{d_o}$ denotes the observed covariates, $Y\in \mathbb{R}$ denotes the outcome variable, and $X \in \mathcal{X} := [0,1]^{d_x}$ denotes the treatment variable.
nodes.statement_short: $P$ is the joint law of $(Z,O,X,Y)$ with instrument $Z\in[0,1]^{d_z}$, covariates $O\in[0,1]^{d_o}$, treatment $X\in[0,1]^{d_x}$, outcome $Y\in\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Density notation p
nodes.statement: We use $p$ to denote the probability density functions; for example, $p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z, \mathbf o)$ denotes the density of the conditional distribution $P_{X\mid Z=\mathbf z, O=\mathbf o}$.

nodes.name: Conditional expectation operator T
nodes.statement_short: $T:L^2(P_{XO})\to L^2(P_{ZO})$, $f\mapsto \mathbb{E}[f(X,O)\mid Z,O]$ written as an integral against $p(x|z,o)$.

nodes.name: Natural numbers notation
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{N}_{+}$ denote the set of positive integers and $\mathbb{N}=\mathbb{N}_{+} \cup\{0\}$ denote the set of non-negative integers.

nodes.name: L^p(P) spaces
nodes.statement: For a distribution $P$ defined on a measurable space $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{X}))$ and $0

nodes.name: L^p of the Lebesgue measure
nodes.statement: When $P$ is the Lebesgue measure $\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}$ over $\mathcal{X}$, we write $L^p(\mathcal{X}) := L^p\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{X}}\right)$.

nodes.name: Bochner space L^p(X;H)
nodes.statement: For $H$ a separable Hilbert space, we let $L^p(\mathcal{X};H)$ denote the space of Bochner 2-integrable functions from $\mathcal{X}$ to $H$ with norm $\|F\|^2_{L^2(\mathcal{X}; H)} = \int_{\mathcal{X}}\|F(\mathbf x)\|^2_{H}\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x$.

nodes.name: Isometric isomorphism
nodes.statement: Two Banach spaces $E_1,E_2$ are said to be isometrically isomorphic, denoted $E_1\cong E_2$, if there exists an isometric isomorphism $S$, such that $\| S h\|_{E_2} = \|h \|_{E_1}$ for all $h \in E_1$.

nodes.name: Norm equivalence
nodes.statement: Two Banach spaces $E_1,E_2$ are said to be norm equivalent, denoted $E_1\simeq E_2$, if $E_1,E_2$ coincide as sets and there are constants $c_1, c_2>0$ such that $c_1\|h\|_{E_1} \leq\|h\|_{E_2} \leq c_2\|h\|_{E_1}$ holds for all $h \in E_1$.

nodes.name: Operator norm and adjoint notation
nodes.statement: For an operator $T: E_1 \rightarrow E_2$, $\|T\|$ denotes its operator norm and $T^\ast$ denotes its adjoint.

nodes.name: Hilbert-Schmidt operator space S_2
nodes.statement: For two Hilbert spaces $H_1, H_2$, $S_2(H_1, H_2)$ is the Hilbert space of Hilbert-Schmidt operators from $H_1$ to $H_2$.

nodes.name: Min/max notation
nodes.statement: For two numbers $\alpha$ and $\beta$, we let $\alpha \wedge \beta=\min (\alpha, \beta)$ and $\alpha \vee \beta=\max (\alpha, \beta)$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic inequality notation
nodes.statement: $\lesssim$ (resp. $\gtrsim$) means $\leq$ (resp. $\geq$) up to positive multiplicative constants.

nodes.name: Sample splitting: datasets D_1 and D_2
nodes.statement: In Stage I, we learn the conditional expectation operator $T$ with dataset $\mathcal{D}_1 := \{(\tilde{\mathbf z}_{i}, \tilde{\mathbf o}_i, \tilde{\mathbf x}_i)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:hat_F_xi}); in Stage II, \steve{we perform regression of the outcome $Y$ on the features learned in Stage I with dataset $\mathcal{D}_2 := \{(\mathbf z_i, \mathbf o_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:hat_f_lambda}).}

nodes.name: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS)
nodes.statement: For a domain $\mathcal{X}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{d}$, a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ of functions $f:\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$ is called a \emph{Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space} (RKHS) if the evaluation functional $\delta_{\mathbf x}:\mathcal{H} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f \mapsto f(\mathbf x)$ is continuous for every $\mathbf x\in \mathcal{X}$.
differentia: the evaluation functional $\delta_{\mathbf x}:\mathcal{H} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f \mapsto f(\mathbf x)$ is continuous for every $\mathbf x\in \mathcal{X}$

nodes.name: Reproducing kernel and reproducing property
nodes.statement: Every RKHS $\mathcal{H}$ has a unique symmetric, positive definite \emph{reproducing kernel} $k : \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}$, which satisfies $k(\mathbf x,\cdot)\in \mathcal{H}$ for all $\mathbf x\in \mathcal{X}$ and $\langle f, k(\cdot, \mathbf x)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} = f(\mathbf x)$ for all $f\in \mathcal{H}$ and $\mathbf x\in \mathcal{X}$ (the reproducing property).

nodes.name: RKHSs H_X, H_{O,1}, H_{O,2}, H_Z
nodes.statement: To describe the KIV-O algorithm, we introduce RKHSs $\mathcal{H}_X$ on $\mathcal{X}$, $\mathcal{H}_{O,1}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{O,2}$ on $\mathcal{O}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{Z}$ on $\mathcal{Z}$.

nodes.name: Kernels k_X, k_{O,1}, k_{O,2}, k_Z
nodes.statement: We denote the associated unique reproducing kernels via $k_{X}: \mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{X}\to \mathbb{R}, k_{O,1} : \mathcal{O}\times \mathcal{O}\to \mathbb{R}, k_{O,2}: \mathcal{O}\times \mathcal{O}\to \mathbb{R}, k_{Z} : \mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{Z}\to \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Canonical feature maps
nodes.statement: We denote the canonical feature map of $\mathcal{H}_{X}$ as $\phi_{X}(\mathbf x) := k_{X}(\mathbf x,\cdot)$, and similarly for feature maps $\phi_{O,1}, \phi_{O,2}, \phi_{Z}$.

nodes.name: Measurable bounded kernels
nodes.statement: All kernels ($k_X, k_{O,1}, k_{O,2}$ and $k_{Z}$) are measurable and bounded.
nodes.label: ass: kernel_technical

nodes.name: Embedding I_{P_X} is compact and Hilbert-Schmidt
nodes.statement: An immediate consequence of \Cref{ass: kernel_technical} is that the embedding $I_{P_{X}} : \mathcal{H}_{X} \to L^2(P_{X})$, which maps a function $f\in \mathcal{H}_{X}$ to its $P_{X}$-equivalence class $[f]_{P_{X}}$ is well-defined, compact and Hilbert-Schmidt~\citep[Lemma 2.3]{steinwart2012mercer}.
assumptions: \Cref{ass: kernel_technical}
conclusions: the embedding $I_{P_{X}} : \mathcal{H}_{X} \to L^2(P_{X})$, which maps a function $f\in \mathcal{H}_{X}$ to its $P_{X}$-equivalence class $[f]_{P_{X}}$ is well-defined, compact and Hilbert-Schmidt

nodes.name: Image space [H_X]_{P_X}
nodes.statement: We define $[\mathcal{H}_X]_{P_X} \subseteq L^2(P_X)$ as the image of $I_{P_{X}}$.

nodes.name: Power space
nodes.statement: For $\beta>0$, we denote by $[\mathcal{H}_X]_{P_X}^\beta$ the $\beta$-th \emph{power space}, as introduced in \citet[Theorem 4.6]{steinwart2012mercer}.

nodes.name: Power spaces are interpolation spaces
nodes.statement: For $0\leq \beta\leq 1$, this space is shown to be isomorphic to the $\beta$-interpolation space $[L^2(P_X),[\mathcal{H}_X]_{P_X}]_{\beta, 2}$ \citep[Theorem 4.6]{steinwart2012mercer}.
assumptions: For $0\leq \beta\leq 1$
conclusions: this space is shown to be isomorphic to the $\beta$-interpolation space $[L^2(P_X),[\mathcal{H}_X]_{P_X}]_{\beta, 2}$

nodes.name: 1-interpolation space is isometric to (ker I)^perp
nodes.statement: It is known that the $1$-interpolation space $[\mathcal{H}_X]_{P_X}^{1}$ is isometrically isomorphic to the closed subspace $(\operatorname{ker} I_{P_{X}})^{\perp}$ of $\mathcal{H}_X$ via $I_{P_{X}}$~\citep[Lemma 2.12]{steinwart2012mercer}.
conclusions: the $1$-interpolation space $[\mathcal{H}_X]_{P_X}^{1}$ is isometrically isomorphic to the closed subspace $(\operatorname{ker} I_{P_{X}})^{\perp}$ of $\mathcal{H}_X$ via $I_{P_{X}}$

nodes.name: Tensor product Hilbert space
nodes.statement:
For two Hilbert spaces $H,H'$, we let $H\otimes H'$ denote their tensor product Hilbert space, defined as 
$H\otimes H' := \overline{\mathrm{span}\{u\otimes u':u\in H,u'\in H'\}}$, 
where $u\otimes u'$ is the linear rank-one operator $H'\rightarrow H$ defined by $(u\otimes u') v' = \langle u', v' \rangle_{H'} u$ \citep[Section 12]{aubin2011applied}.

nodes.name: Product RKHSs H_{ZO,1} and H_{XO,2}
nodes.statement: In the case of RKHSs, the tensor product $\mathcal{H}_{ZO,1} := \mathcal{H}_Z \otimes \mathcal{H}_{O,1}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{XO,2} := \mathcal{H}_{X} \otimes \mathcal{H}_{O,2}$ are the unique RKHSs associated with the product kernels $k_{ZO,1}((\mathbf z,\mathbf o), (\mathbf z',\mathbf o')) = k_{Z}(\mathbf z,\mathbf z') \cdot k_{O,1}(\mathbf o,\mathbf o')$ and $k_{XO,2}((\mathbf x,\mathbf o), (\mathbf x',\mathbf o')) = k_{X}(\mathbf x,\mathbf x') \cdot k_{O,2}(\mathbf o,\mathbf o')$, respectively~\citep{berlinet2004reproducing}.

nodes.name: Embedding I_{P_{XO,2}} and its power spaces
nodes.statement: We define the embedding $I_{P_{XO,2}} : \mathcal{H}_{XO,2} \to L^2(P_{XO})$ which maps a function $f\in \mathcal{H}_{XO,2}$ to its $P_{XO}$-equivalence class $[f]_{P_{XO}}$, and define the $\beta$-th power spaces as $[\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}]_{P_{XO}}^\beta$.

nodes.name: Equivalence-class bracket notation
nodes.statement: In the rest of the paper, we omit the subscript and use the notation $[\cdot]$ to denote equivalence classes in $L^2$.

nodes.name: KIV-O algorithm
nodes.statement:
We are now ready to present the KIV-O algorithm. \\  
\indent \textit{Stage I.} The action of the operator $T$ on the RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}$ can be represented with the aid of the \emph{conditional mean embedding} (CME)~\citep{song2009hilbert, park2021measuretheoreticapproachkernelconditional, klebanov2020rigorous, lietal2022optimal}. We define the CME $F_{\ast}$ as the mapping from $\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}$ to $\mathcal{H}_{X}$, given by $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\phi_{X}(X)\mid Z = \mathbf z,O = \mathbf o]$. Equipped with the CME, we note that the image of $T$ acting on a function $f\in \mathcal{H}_{XO,2}$ admits the following representation: for any $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\in \mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}$,
\begin{align*}
    &(Tf)(\mathbf z,\mathbf o) = \mathbb{E}[f(X,O)\mid Z=\mathbf z, O = \mathbf o] = \mathbb{E}[\langle f, \phi_{X}(X) \otimes \phi_{O,2}(O)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}} \mid Z = \mathbf z, O = \mathbf o]\\
    &= \langle f, \mathbb{E}[\phi_{X}(X)\mid Z = \mathbf z, O = \mathbf o]\otimes \phi_{O,2}(\mathbf o)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}} = \langle f, F_{\ast}(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\otimes \phi_{O,2}(\mathbf o)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}},
\end{align*}
where the second equality follows from the \emph{reproducing property} and the third equality requires a Bochner integrable feature map $\phi_X$ (true for bounded kernels) from \Cref{ass: kernel_technical}~\citep[Definition A.5.20]{steinwart2008support}. 
Note that the feature map $\phi_{X}$ is projected by the conditional expectation of the conditional distribution $P_{X\mid Z,O}$, while the feature map $\phi_{O,2}$ remains unprojected. This is the key distinction from classical KIV. 
In Stage I, our goal is to estimate the CME, $F_{\ast}$, by performing a regularized least squares regression in a vector-valued RKHS $\mathcal{G}$ induced by the operator-valued kernel ~\citep{grunewalder2012conditional, lietal2022optimal} 
\begin{align} K := k_{ZO,1}\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{H}_X} : (\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O})\times (\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O})\to \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{X}),
\end{align}
where $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{X})$ denotes the space of bounded linear operators $\mathcal{H}_{X}\to \mathcal{H}_{X}$, and $\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{H}_{X}}\in \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{X})$ denotes the identity operator on $\mathcal{H}_{X}$. 
An important property of $\mathcal{G}$ is that it is isometrically isomorphic to the space $S_2(\mathcal{H}_{Z O, 1}, \mathcal{H}_X)$ of Hilbert-Schmidt operators from $\mathcal{H}_{Z O, 1}$ to $\mathcal{H}_X$. On the other hand, by \citet[Theorem 12.6.1]{aubin2011applied}, $S_2(L^2(P_{ZO}), \mathcal{H}_X)$ is isometrically isomorphic to the Bochner space $L^2(P_{ZO}, \mathcal{H}_X)$, and we denote this isomorphism as $\Psi$. 
We can define vector-valued $\beta$-th power spaces~\citep[Definition 4]{lietal2022optimal}:
\begin{talign} [\mathcal{G}]^\beta := \Psi\left(S_2\left([\mathcal{H}_{ZO,1}]^\beta, \mathcal{H}_{X} \right)\right)=\left\{F \mid F=\Psi(C), C \in S_2\left([\mathcal{H}_{ZO,1}]^\beta, \mathcal{H}_{X} \right)\right\} .
\end{talign}
The space $[\mathcal{G}]^\beta$ generalizes the definition of scalar-valued \emph{power space} to vector-valued RKHSs, quantifying the smoothness of $F_\ast$ relative to the RKHS $\mathcal{G}$ (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:F_ast_power_space}). We refer the reader to \citet{carmeli2006vector, carmeli2010vector} for definitions and properties of more general vector-valued RKHSs. 

Given $\mathcal{D}_1 = \{(\tilde{\mathbf z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf o}_i, \tilde{\mathbf x}_i)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}}$ sampled i.i.d from
the joint distribution $P_{XZO}$, a regularized estimator of $F_\ast$ is obtained as the solution to the following optimization problem:
\begin{talign} \hat{F}_{\xi} := \underset{F \in \mathcal{G}}{arg\,min } \frac{1}{\tilde{n}} \sum_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}} \left\|\phi_{X}(\tilde{\mathbf x}_i) - F(\tilde{\mathbf z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf o}_i)\right\|_{\mathcal{H}_{X}}^2 + \xi\|F\|_{\mathcal{G}}^2,
\end{talign}
where $\xi >0 $ denotes the Stage I regularization parameter. 

\textit{Stage II.} In Stage II, we perform regularized least squares regression in the RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}$, using features derived from the estimated conditional mean embedding $\hat{F}_{\xi}$. Specifically, the features are $\hat{F}_{\xi}(Z, O) \otimes \phi_{O,2}(O)$.
Given $\mathcal{D}_2 = \{(\mathbf z_i,\mathbf o_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$ i.i.d sampled from the joint distribution $P_{ZOY}$ and independent of $\mathcal{D}_1$, the regularized estimator $\hat{f}_{\lambda}$ is defined as: 
\begin{talign} \hat{f}_{\lambda} &:= \underset{f\in \mathcal{H}_{XO,2}}{arg\,min}  \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \left\langle f, \hat{F}_{\xi}(\mathbf z_i,\mathbf o_i) \otimes \phi_{O,2}(\mathbf o_i) \right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}} \right)^2 + \lambda \|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{X}\otimes \mathcal{H}_{O,2}},
\end{talign}
where $\lambda >0 $ denotes the Stage II regularization parameter.\footnote{The naive extension to observed covariates in KIV \citet{singh2019kernel} considers augmenting $X,Z$ to $(X,O), (Z,O)$. This approach is not consistent because Stage I would then require estimating the conditional mean embedding $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\phi_X(X)\otimes\phi_O(O)\mid Z=\mathbf z,O=\mathbf o]$, which is \emph{not} Hilbert-Schmidt and for which vector-valued kernel ridge regression is not consistent, see also \citep[Appendix B.9]{mastouri2021proximal} for an illustration.}
nodes.statement_short: Kernel 2SLS with covariates: Stage I estimates the conditional mean embedding by vector-valued KRR; Stage II regresses $Y$ on $\hat F_\xi(Z,O)\otimes\phi_{O,2}(O)$ by KRR.

nodes.name: Conditional mean embedding F_*
nodes.statement: We define the CME $F_{\ast}$ as the mapping from $\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}$ to $\mathcal{H}_{X}$, given by $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\mapsto \mathbb{E}[\phi_{X}(X)\mid Z = \mathbf z,O = \mathbf o]$.

nodes.name: CME representation of T on H_{XO,2}
nodes.statement_short: For $f\in\mathcal{H}_{XO,2}$, $(Tf)(z,o)=\langle f, F_*(z,o)\otimes\phi_{O,2}(o)\rangle$ by the reproducing property and Bochner integrability.
assumptions: for any $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\in \mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}$
conclusions: the image of $T$ acting on a function $f\in \mathcal{H}_{XO,2}$ admits the following representation

nodes.name: Vector-valued RKHS G and operator-valued kernel K
Operator-valued kernel K (eq:op_val_kernel)
nodes.statement: K := k_{ZO,1}\mathrm{Id}_{\mathcal{H}_X} : (\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O})\times (\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O})\to \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{H}_{X}),
nodes.label: eq:op_val_kernel

nodes.name: G is isometric to Hilbert-Schmidt operators
nodes.statement: An important property of $\mathcal{G}$ is that it is isometrically isomorphic to the space $S_2(\mathcal{H}_{Z O, 1}, \mathcal{H}_X)$ of Hilbert-Schmidt operators from $\mathcal{H}_{Z O, 1}$ to $\mathcal{H}_X$.
conclusions: it is isometrically isomorphic to the space $S_2(\mathcal{H}_{Z O, 1}, \mathcal{H}_X)$ of Hilbert-Schmidt operators from $\mathcal{H}_{Z O, 1}$ to $\mathcal{H}_X$

nodes.name: Isomorphism Psi to the Bochner space
nodes.statement: On the other hand, by \citet[Theorem 12.6.1]{aubin2011applied}, $S_2(L^2(P_{ZO}), \mathcal{H}_X)$ is isometrically isomorphic to the Bochner space $L^2(P_{ZO}, \mathcal{H}_X)$, and we denote this isomorphism as $\Psi$.

nodes.name: Vector-valued power space [G]^beta
L2(P_XO)-risk
L2 risk of KIV-O (eq:L2_risk)
nodes.statement: \|\hat{f}_\lambda - f_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{XO})}.
nodes.label: eq:L2_risk

nodes.name: Multi-indices
nodes.statement: Let $(\mathbb{N}^{+})^{d}$ be the set of all multi-indices $\boldsymbol\alpha = (\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d)$ with $\alpha_i\in \mathbb{N}$ and $|\boldsymbol\alpha| = \sum_{i=1}^{d}\alpha_i$.

nodes.name: Classical and weak partial derivatives
nodes.statement: For $\boldsymbol\alpha\in \mathbb{N}^{d}$ and $f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$,  $\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}$ denotes the classical (pointwise) partial derivative, and $D^{\boldsymbol\alpha} f$ denotes the corresponding weak (distributional) partial derivative.

nodes.name: Smooth conditional density (order m_o in o, m_z in z)
nodes.statement: Let $m_o, m_z \in \mathbb{N}^+$. For any $\mathbf x\in\mathcal{X}$, the map $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\mapsto p(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf z,\mathbf o)$ has bounded, continuous derivatives of order $m_o$ with respect to $\mathbf o$ and order $m_z$ with respect to $\mathbf z$ on the interior of $\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}$. \begin{align*} \rho := \max_{|\boldsymbol\alpha|\leq m_z}\max_{|\boldsymbol\beta|\leq m_o}\sup_{\mathbf x \in \mathcal{X} ,\mathbf z\in\mathcal{Z},\mathbf o\in\mathcal{O}} \left|\partial^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z}\partial^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)\right|< \infty. \end{align*}
nodes.label: assn: technical

nodes.name: Vector-valued dominating mixed-smoothness Sobolev space
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space. Let $m_z,m_o\in \mathbb{N}^+$. We define \begin{align*} MW^{m_z,m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}; H):=\left\{ F \mid F \in L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}; H), \|F\|_{MW^{m_z,m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}; H)} <\infty \right\} . \end{align*} where $\|F\|_{MW^{m_z,m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}; H)} := \sum_{|\boldsymbol\alpha|\leq m_z}\sum_{|\boldsymbol\beta|\leq m_o} \| D^{\boldsymbol\alpha}_{\mathbf z} D^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o} F \|_{L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}; H)}$.
nodes.statement_short: $MW^{m_z,m_o}_2$: $H$-valued $L^2$ functions whose mixed weak derivatives up to order $m_z$ in $z$ and $m_o$ in $o$ are in $L^2$.

nodes.name: CME lies in mixed-smoothness Sobolev space
nodes.statement: \Cref{assn: technical} implies that $\|D_{\mathbf z}^{\boldsymbol\alpha}D^{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathbf o}F_{\ast}\|_{L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X})}$ is bounded for any multi-indices  $|\boldsymbol\alpha|\leq m_z$ and $|\boldsymbol\beta|\leq m_o$. Hence, $F_{\ast}\in MW^{m_z, m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X})$.
assumptions: \Cref{assn: technical}
conclusions: $F_{\ast}\in MW^{m_z, m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_{X})$

nodes.name: Choice of Stage I kernels (Sobolev/Matérn)
nodes.statement: \steve{We let $k_{Z}$ and $k_{O, 1}$ be any positive definite kernels} such that their associated RKHSs \steve{$\mathcal{H}_{Z}, \mathcal{H}_{O,1}$} are \steve{respectively} norm equivalent to real-valued Sobolev spaces $W_2^{t_z}(\mathcal{Z})$ and $W_2^{t_o}(\mathcal{O})$, where $t_z > \frac{d_z}{2},t_o > \frac{d_o}{2}$. Following \cite{chen2025nested}, we say that $k_{Z}, k_{O, 1}$ are Sobolev reproducing kernels of smoothness $t_z, t_o$. An important example of Sobolev reproducing kernel is the Matérn-$\nu$ kernel whose RKHS is norm equivalent to a Sobolev space $W^{t}_2$ of smoothness $t = \nu+d/2$~\citep[Corollary 10.48]{wendland2004scattered}. Since all Sobolev reproducing kernels are bounded and measurable, $k_{Z}, k_{O,1}$ satisfy \Cref{ass: kernel_technical}. With the above choice of $k_Z$ and $k_{O,1}$, it follows from \Cref{lem:equivalence_G} that the vector-valued RKHS $\mathcal{G}$ associated with the operator-valued kernel in Eq.~\eqref{eq:op_val_kernel} is norm equivalent to the mixed-smoothness Sobolev space $MW^{t_z,t_o}(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_X)$. Since $F_\ast \in MW^{m_z,m_o}_2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_X)$ as established above, $F_\ast$ lies in the appropriate power space of $\mathcal{G}$ for suitably chosen $(t_z,t_o)$. Consequently, \citet{lietal2022optimal,meunier2024optimalratesvectorvaluedspectral} show that estimating the CME via Eq.~\eqref{eq:hat_F_xi} achieves the minimax-optimal rate in both the $L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H}_X)$ and $\mathcal{G}$ norms, provided that the regularization parameter $\xi$ is selected adaptively with respect to the sample size $\tilde{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Stage I kernels are Sobolev reproducing kernels (e.g. Matérn); then $\mathcal{G}$ is norm-equivalent to a mixed Sobolev space and CME regression is minimax optimal.
nodes.label: rem:kernel_stage_1_choice

nodes.name: Modulus of smoothness
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathcal{X} = \prod_{i=1}^d \mathcal{X}^{(i)} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ be a subset with non-empty interior, $
u$ be a product measure on $\mathcal{X}$ with $
u=\otimes_{i=1}^d 
u_i$, and $f: \mathcal{X} ightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function in $L^p(
u)$ for some $p \in (0, \infty]$. The $r$-th modulus of smoothness of $f$ is defined by  egin{talign} \omega_{r, p}\left(f,  oldsymbol{t}, \mathcal{X} ight) = \sup _{0<\left|h_iight| \leq t_i} \left\|	riangle_{ oldsymbol{h}}^{r}f ight\|_{L^p\left(
uight)}, \end{talign} where the $r$-th difference of $f$ in the direction $ oldsymbol{h}$ at point $\mathbf x$, denoted as $	riangle_{ oldsymbol{h}}^{r} f \left( \mathbf x ight)$, is defined through recursion: $\Delta_{ oldsymbol{h}}^0 f(\mathbf x) :=f(\mathbf x)$ and $\Delta_{ oldsymbol{h}}^r f(\mathbf x) :=\Delta_{ oldsymbol{h}}^{r-1} f(\mathbf x+ oldsymbol{h})-\Delta_{ oldsymbol{h}}^{r-1} f(\mathbf x)$ if $\mathbf x, \mathbf x+ oldsymbol{h}, \ldots, \mathbf x+r  oldsymbol{h} \in \mathcal{X}$ and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: $\omega_{r,p}(f,t)$ is the sup over $|h_i|\le t_i$ of the $L^p$ norm of the $r$-th finite difference of $f$.
nodes.label: eq:module_smoothness

nodes.name: Anisotropic Besov space
nodes.statement:
For $p \in[1, \infty), q \in[1, \infty]$ and $ oldsymbol{s}=\left(s_1, \ldots, s_dight) \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^d$, the anisotropic Besov space $B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}(
u)$ is defined by  egin{talign} B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}(
u):=\left\{f \in L^p(
u): \|f\|_{B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}(
u)} := \|f\|_{L^p(
u)} + |f|_{B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}\left(
uight)}<\inftyight\} , \end{talign} where the Besov semi-norm $|f|_{B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}\left(
uight)}$ is defined as,  egin{talign} |f|_{B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}\left(
uight)} := \left[ \int_0^1\left[t^{-1} \omega_{r, p} \left(f, t^{1 / s_1}, \ldots, t^{1 / s_d}, \mathcal{X} ight)ight]^q \; rac{\mathrm{d}t}{t}ight]^{1 / q}, \end{talign} for $r = \max\{ \lfloor s_1 floor, \ldots, \lfloor s_d floor \} + 1$. When $q = \infty$, we replace the integral by a supremum in Eq. \eqref{eq:besov_semi_norm}. When $
u$ is the Lebesgue measure over $\mathcal{X}$, we use the notation $B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}(\mathcal{X}) := B_{p, q}^{ oldsymbol{s}}(
u)$.
nodes.statement_short: $B^{\mathbf s}_{p,q}$: $L^p$ functions with finite anisotropic Besov seminorm defined via the modulus of smoothness at scales $t^{1/s_i}$.
nodes.label: defi:abs

nodes.name: Besov space B^{s_x,s_o}_{2,inf}
nodes.statement: In other words, we only consider $\boldsymbol{s}=(s_x,\dots,s_x, s_o,\dots,s_o) \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d_x+d_0}$ and denote $B^{\boldsymbol{s}}_{2,\infty}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O})$ as $B^{s_x, s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O})$.

nodes.name: Unit ball U
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{U}(B^{s_x,s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}))$ denote the unit ball of $B^{s_x,s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})$ with respect to the Besov norm.

nodes.name: Continuous functions C^0
nodes.statement: Let $C^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})$ denote the space of continuous functions $\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}\to \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Anisotropic Besov smoothness of f* (class S)
nodes.statement: $f_{\ast}\in \mathfrak{S}$ where we define $\mathfrak{S} := \mathbb{U}(B^{s_x,s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}))\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}) \cap L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})\cap C^{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})$.
nodes.label: ass:f_ast

nodes.name: f* has L2 norm at most 1
nodes.statement: In particular, under \Cref{ass:f_ast}, $\|f_{\ast}\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})} \leq \|f_{\ast}\|_{B^{s_x,s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})}\leq 1$.
assumptions: under \Cref{ass:f_ast}
conclusions: $\|f_{\ast}\|_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})} \leq \|f_{\ast}\|_{B^{s_x,s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o})}\leq 1$

nodes.name: Choice of Stage II kernels (anisotropic Gaussian)
nodes.statement: We choose $k_X$ and $k_{O,2}$ to be Gaussian kernels $k_{\gamma_x}$ and $k_{\gamma_o}$ with bandwidths $\gamma_x\in (0,1), \gamma_o\in (0,1)$. Denote $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x}$ and $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_o}$ as the associated Gaussian RKHSs; $\phi_{\gamma_x}$ and $\phi_{\gamma_o}$ as the associated feature maps. The tensor product RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o} := \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x} \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_o}$ is the unique RKHS associated with the product kernel \begin{talign} k_{\gamma_x}(\mathbf x,\mathbf x') \cdot k_{\gamma_o}(\mathbf o,\mathbf o') = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{d_x}\frac{(x_j - x_j')^2}{\gamma_x^2} - \sum_{j=1}^{d_o}\frac{(o_j - o_j')^2}{\gamma_o^2}\right). \end{talign} This kernel is called an anisotropic Gaussian kernel and its associated RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$ is the corresponding anisotropic Gaussian RKHS. \citet{hang2021optimal} proves that kernel ridge regression with anisotropic Gaussian kernel in the form of Eq.~\eqref{eq:anis_gaussian_kernel} is minimax optimal for anisotropic Besov space target functions, provided that both the regularization parameter and the kernel lengthscale $\gamma_x, \gamma_o$ are \emph{adaptive} to the number of samples $n$. Such adaptivity will also be evident in our setting (see \Cref{thm:upper_rate}). \citet{singh2019kernel} adopt the median heuristic for selecting the kernel lengthscale in KIV algorithm, a widely used practical choice. Unlike ours, however, the theoretical relationship between their heuristic and the underlying smoothness of the target function remains unclear.
nodes.statement_short: Stage II uses Gaussian kernels with separate lengthscales $\gamma_x,\gamma_o$ (anisotropic Gaussian RKHS), known to be minimax optimal for anisotropic Besov targets in KRR.
nodes.label: rem:kernel_stage_2_choice

nodes.name: Why different kernels in Stage I and Stage II
nodes.statement: We briefly explain the rationale for selecting different types of kernels for Stage I and Stage II. For Stage I, the regression target is the conditional mean embedding $F_\ast$. By \Cref{assn: technical}, we have shown that $F_{\ast}$ belongs to the mixed Sobolev space $MW^{m_z,m_o}(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O};\mathcal{H})$, which can be learned at the minimax optimal rate using a tensor-product Sobolev RKHS (see \Cref{prop:cme_rate}). On the other hand, the Stage II regression target $f_\ast$ belongs to an anisotropic Besov space (\Cref{ass:f_ast}). \citet{hang2021optimal} has proved that learning an anisotropic function in a nonparametric regression setting is minimax optimal via an anisotropic Gaussian RKHS. We have followed their approach with additional refinements to our setting, that reveals the interplay between the effect of $T$ and the anisotropic smoothness of $f_{\ast}$. See \Cref{sec:theory} for the details.
nodes.label: rem:choice_kernel

nodes.name: Stability and link conditions fail for NPIV-O
nodes.statement:
In the introduction, we outlined two challenges for the theoretical analysis of NPIV-O. The first challenge concerns the fact that $T$ is an identity operator restricted to the infinite dimensional function space $\mathcal{F}_1$ (defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:calF_1_espace}). This has the following consequences. The $L^2$-\emph{stability condition} imposed in the NPIV literature (cf. \citet[Assumption 6]{blundell2007semi}, \citet[Assumption 5.2(ii)]{chen2012estimation} and \citet[Assumption 4.2]{Chen_2018}) fails to hold except for the degenerate case where the sieve measure of ill-posedness is $1$ (i.e. $Z=X$, see also \Cref{rem:partial_smoothing}). The \emph{link condition} imposed in the optimal rate literature for NPIV (cf. \citet{HallHorowitz2005}, \citet[Assumption 2.2]{chen2011rate}, \citet[Condition LB]{Chen_2018}) implies that $\|T f\|_{L^2 (P_{Z O})} \leq \|B^r f\|_{L^2(P_{X O})}$ for some known compact operator $B$, where a larger $r$ corresponds to a more ill-posed model. However, for any $f \in \mathcal{F}_1$ defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:calF_1_espace}, we have $
\|T f\|_{L^2(P_{Z O})}=\|f\|_{L^2(P_{X O})}$ so the link condition only holds with $r = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Because $T$ is the identity on $\mathcal{F}_1$, the $L^2$-stability condition and link condition of NPIV theory only hold in degenerate cases.

nodes.name: L-infinity completeness (bounded completeness)
nodes.statement: The conditional distribution $P_{X\mid Z,O}$ satisfies that, for every bounded measurable function $f:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O}\to\mathbb{R}$, if $\mathbb{E}[f(X,O)\mid Z, O] = 0$ holds $P_{ZO}$-almost surely, then $f(X,O)=0$ holds $P_{XO}$-almost surely.
nodes.label: ass:T_injective

nodes.name: Fourier transform on L^1
nodes.statement:
For $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^{d_x})$, its Fourier transform is defined as a Lebesgue integral \citep[9.1]{rudin1987real}: 
$\hat{f}(\cdot) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}f(\mathbf x)\exp(-i\langle \mathbf x,\cdot\rangle)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x$.

nodes.name: Unitary Fourier operator F on L^2
nodes.statement:
One can extend the Fourier transform to $L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x})$ by defining it as a \emph{unitary} operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x})$~\citep[Theorem 9.13]{rudin1987real}. 
We use $\mathcal{F}$ to denote this operator, and let $\mathcal{F}^{-1}$ denote its inverse.

nodes.name: Low- and high-frequency function sets LF(gamma), HF(gamma)
nodes.statement:
For any scalar $\gamma\in (0,1)$, we define the following two sets of functions:
\begin{talign} \begin{aligned}
\mathrm{LF}(\gamma) := \{ f : \mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o} \to \mathbb{R} \ \Big| \ 
& \forall \mathbf o \in \mathcal{O}, \; [f(\cdot, \mathbf o)] \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x}), \\
& \;\mathrm{supp}\big(\mathcal{F}[f(\cdot, \mathbf o)]\big) 
\subseteq \{ \boldsymbol{\omega}_x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_x} : \|\boldsymbol{\omega}_x\|_2 \leq \gamma^{-1} \} \}.\\
\mathrm{HF}(\gamma) := \{ f : \mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o} \to \mathbb{R} \ \Big| \ 
& \forall \mathbf o \in \mathcal{O}, \; [f(\cdot, \mathbf o)] \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x}), \\
& \;\mathrm{supp}\big(\mathcal{F}[f(\cdot, \mathbf o)]\big) 
\subseteq \{ \boldsymbol{\omega}_x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_x} : \|\boldsymbol{\omega}_x\|_2 \geq \gamma^{-1} \} \}.
\end{aligned}
\end{talign}
where $\mathrm{supp}$ for an element of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^{d_x})$ is defined in \Cref{defi:fn_dist} and \Cref{defi:supp_dist} in the Supplementary.
nodes.statement_short: LF($\gamma$)/HF($\gamma$): functions whose partial Fourier transform in $x$ is supported inside/outside the ball of radius $\gamma^{-1}$, for every $o$.

nodes.name: Fourier measure of partial ill-posedness of T
nodes.statement: There exists a constant $c_0>0$ and a parameter $\eta_0\in [0,\infty)$ depending only on $T$, such that for all $\gamma \in (0,1)$ and all functions $f \in \mathrm{LF}(\gamma) \cap L^\infty(P_{XO})$, the following inequality is satisfied: \begin{align*} \|Tf\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})} \geq c_0\gamma^{d_x\eta_0} \|f\|_{L^2(P_{XO})}. \end{align*} In particular, $c_0$ does not depend on $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: For $f\in$ LF($\gamma$), $\|Tf\|\ge c_0\gamma^{d_x\eta_0}\|f\|$: $T$ shrinks low $x$-frequencies at most polynomially.
nodes.label: ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness

nodes.name: Fourier measure of partial contractivity of T
nodes.statement: There exists a constant $c_1>0$ and a parameter $\eta_1\in [0,\infty)$ depending only on $T$, such that for all $\gamma \in (0,1)$ and all functions $f \in \mathrm{HF}(\gamma) \cap L^\infty(P_{XO})$, the following inequality is satisfied: \begin{align*} \|Tf\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})} \leq c_1\gamma^{d_x\eta_1} \|f\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} . \end{align*} In particular, $c_1$ does not depend on $\gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: For $f\in$ HF($\gamma$), $\|Tf\|\le c_1\gamma^{d_x\eta_1}\|f\|$: $T$ smooths high $x$-frequencies polynomially.
nodes.label: ass:T_contractivity

nodes.name: eta_0 >= eta_1 and c_0 <= c_1
nodes.statement: If Assumption \ref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} and \ref{ass:T_contractivity} hold simultaneously, and $P_{XO}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O}$, then $\eta_0\geq \eta_1$ and $c_0\leq c_1$ (\Cref{lem:eta_0_eta_1_appendix} in \Cref{sec:appendix_examples}).
assumptions: Assumption \ref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} and \ref{ass:T_contractivity} hold simultaneously
$P_{XO}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O}$
conclusions: $\eta_0\geq \eta_1$ and $c_0\leq c_1$

nodes.name: Kernel L(x,x';o) of T*T
nodes.statement:
To motivate the partial smoothing effect of $T$, notice that the bounded self-adjoint operator $T^{\ast}T: L^2(P_{XO}) \to L^2(P_{XO})$ acts on $f\in L^2(P_{XO})$ as follows:
\begin{align} ((T^{\ast}T) f)(\mathbf x',\mathbf o) = \int_{\mathcal{X}}f(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x, 
\end{align}
where $L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o):= \int_{\mathcal{Z}}p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z,\mathbf o)p(\mathbf z\mid\mathbf x',\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf z$.
nodes.statement_short: $T^*T$ acts in $x$ as an integral operator with kernel $L(x,x';o)=\int p(x|z,o)p(z|x',o)dz$, separately for each $o$.

nodes.name: Action of T*T (eq:TastT)
nodes.statement: ((T^{\ast}T) f)(\mathbf x',\mathbf o) = \int_{\mathcal{X}}f(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x,
nodes.label: eq:TastT

nodes.name: Subspaces G_X and G_O
T*T is compact on G_X and identity on G_O
nodes.statement:
Under mild conditions on the conditional distribution $p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z, \mathbf o)$~\citep[Assumption A.1]{darolles2011nonparametric}, $T^{\ast}T|_{\mathfrak{G}_{X}}$ 
($T^{\ast}T$ restricted to $\mathfrak{G}_{X}$) is compact and its smoothing effect can be quantified through its eigenvalue decay; while in contrast, $T^{\ast}T|_{\mathfrak{G}_{O}}$ is an identity operator: for $g\in \mathfrak{G}_{O}$
\begin{align} ((T^{\ast}T) g)(\mathbf x, \mathbf o) = \int_{\mathcal{X}}g(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x = \tilde{g}(\mathbf o) \int_{\mathcal{X}}L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x = g(\mathbf x, \mathbf o).
\end{align}
assumptions: Under mild conditions on the conditional distribution $p(\mathbf x\mid \mathbf z, \mathbf o)$~\citep[Assumption A.1]{darolles2011nonparametric}
conclusions:
$T^{\ast}T|_{\mathfrak{G}_{X}}$ 
($T^{\ast}T$ restricted to $\mathfrak{G}_{X}$) is compact and its smoothing effect can be quantified through its eigenvalue decay
$T^{\ast}T|_{\mathfrak{G}_{O}}$ is an identity operator

nodes.name: T*T is the identity on G_O (eq:TTast_mapping)
nodes.statement: ((T^{\ast}T) g)(\mathbf x, \mathbf o) = \int_{\mathcal{X}}g(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x = \tilde{g}(\mathbf o) \int_{\mathcal{X}}L(\mathbf x,\mathbf x';\mathbf o)\;\mathrm{d}\mathbf x = g(\mathbf x, \mathbf o).
nodes.label: eq:TTast_mapping

nodes.name: Connection with sieve measure of ill-posedness
nodes.statement: In this remark, we connect \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} to the sieve measure of ill-posedness condition employed in the analysis of sieve 2SLS~\citep{blundell2007semi, Chen_2018, chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence,kim2025optimality}. For this remark, we omit observed covariates $O$, and take $T : L^2(P_{X})\to L^2(P_{Z})$. The sieve measure of ill-posedness is defined as \begin{align} \tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}} := \sup_{0\neq f\in \Psi_J} \frac{\|f\|_{L^2(P_{X})}}{\|Tf\|_{L^2(P_{Z})}}, \end{align} where $\Psi_J$ denotes the $J$th sieve space for the treatment variable \citep[Section 3]{Chen_2018}. For this remark, we let $\Psi_J$ be the linear span of cardinal B-splines of order $\mathfrak{m}$ up to resolution $\mathfrak{K}$ with $J = (2^{\mathfrak{K}} + \mathfrak{m} + 1)^{d_x} \asymp 2^{\mathfrak{K}d_x}$ \citep[Section 5]{devore1993constructive}. We note that the parameter $\gamma^{-1}$, where $\gamma$ occurs in the definition of the function space $\mathrm{LF}(\gamma)$ in Eq. \eqref{eq:HF_LF}, plays a role analogous to the resolution level $\mathfrak{K}$ for cardinal B-splines. Indeed, $\mathrm{LF}(\gamma)$ for smaller values of $\gamma$ (or $\Psi_J$ for larger values of $J$) correspond to a class of less smooth functions. The above observation and the form of Eq. \eqref{eq:sieve_moip} thus suggests an analogous definition: \begin{align} \tau_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Fourier}} := \sup_{0\neq f\in \mathrm{LF}(\gamma)\cap L^{\infty}(P_{XO})} \frac{\|f\|_{L^2(P_{X})}}{\|Tf\|_{L^2(P_{Z})}}. \end{align} We can thus restate \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} as: there exists a constant $c_0>0$ and a parameter $\eta_0\in [0,\infty)$ depending only on $T$, such that for all $\gamma\in (0,1)$, the following inequality is satisfied: $\tau_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Fourier}}\leq c_0^{-1}\gamma^{-d_x\eta_0}$. In the sieve NPIV literature \citep{blundell2007semi,chen2024adaptiveestimationuniformconfidence, Chen_2018}, an NPIV model is said to be \emph{mildly ill-posed} if $\tau_{J}^{\mathrm{sieve}} = O(J^{\eta}) = O(2^{\eta\mathfrak{K}d_x})$. By the analogy between $\tau_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Fourier}}$ and $\tau_{J}^{\mathrm{sieve}}$, we see that our \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} characterizes a \emph{mildly ill-posed} regime.
nodes.statement_short: Defines a Fourier analogue $\tau^{Fourier}_\gamma$ of the sieve measure of ill-posedness; Assumption 4.2 then says $\tau_\gamma\lesssim\gamma^{-d_x\eta_0}$ (mildly ill-posed).
nodes.label: rem:connection_smoip

nodes.name: Sieve measure of ill-posedness (eq:sieve_moip)
nodes.statement: \tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}} := \sup_{0\neq f\in \Psi_J} \frac{\|f\|_{L^2(P_{X})}}{\|Tf\|_{L^2(P_{Z})}},
nodes.label: eq:sieve_moip

nodes.name: Fourier measure of ill-posedness (eq:kernel_moip)
nodes.statement: \tau_{\gamma}^{\mathrm{Fourier}} := \sup_{0\neq f\in \mathrm{LF}(\gamma)\cap L^{\infty}(P_{XO})} \frac{\|f\|_{L^2(P_{X})}}{\|Tf\|_{L^2(P_{Z})}}.
nodes.label: eq:kernel_moip

nodes.name: Existing treatment of partial smoothing of T in NPIV-O
nodes.statement: Existing work that concerns NPIV-O in the literature circumvents the partial identity structure of $T$ either by imposing additional structural assumptions~\citep{blundell2007semi, syrgkanis2019machine} or by stratifying the problem on $O$~\citep{horowitz2011applied} thereby reducing NPIV-O to NPIV, which is statistically inefficient and scales poorly with the dimension of $O$. Instead of $T$, \citet[Section 3.3]{Chen_2018} consider the compactness and the smoothing effect of the \emph{partial} conditional expectation operator $T_{\mathbf o}: L^2(P_{X\mid O = \mathbf o})\to L^2(P_{Z\mid O=\mathbf o})$ for each $\mathbf o\in \mathcal{O} $. \citet[Section 3.3]{Chen_2018} proves that, if $\Psi_J$ (defined in the above remark) equals the span of the first $J$ eigenvectors of $T_{\mathbf o}^\ast T_{\mathbf o}$ for any $\mathbf o\in\mathcal{O}$, then \begin{align} \tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}} \asymp \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf o\sim O}[\mu_{J, \mathbf o}^2]^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \end{align} where $\mu_{J,\mathbf o}$ is the $J$th singular value of $T_{\mathbf o}$ arranged in non-increasing order. \citet{Chen_2018} then claims that the convergence rates derived for the standard NPIV can be extended to NPIV-O. However, we identify an essential oversight: \citet[Assumption 4 (ii)]{Chen_2018}, which is required for their $L^2$-norm upper bound, cannot hold in the NPIV-O setting. This assumption states that for $\Psi_J$, $f_{\ast}$ satisfies the following inequality: \begin{align*} \tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}}\|T(f_{\ast} - \Pi_J f_{\ast})\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}\leq \|f_{\ast} - \Pi_{J}f_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{XO})}, \end{align*} where $\Pi_J: L^2(P_{XO})\to \Psi_J$ denotes the $L^2$-orthogonal projection from $L^2(P_{XO})$ onto $\Psi_J$. In the NPIV-O setting, if $f_{\ast}$ depends only on $\mathbf o$ and $P_{XO}$ is the Lebesgue measure, then the projection $\Pi_J f_{\ast}$ also depends only on $\mathbf o$. This implies $(T^\ast T)(f_{\ast} - \Pi_J f_{\ast}) = f_{\ast} - \Pi_J f_{\ast}$ as per Eq.~\eqref{eq:TTast_mapping}, forcing ${\tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}}}^{-1} = O(1)$, causing a contradiction with the measure of ill-posedness condition that $\tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}} = \mathcal{O}(J^{\eta_0})$ unless $\eta_0 = 0$. \citet{HallHorowitz2005} addresses NPIV-O by assuming smoothness of $f_\ast(\cdot, \mathbf o)$ relative to $\mathcal{R}(T_{\mathbf o}^\ast T_{\mathbf o})$ for each $\mathbf o\in\mathcal{O}$, which is hard to interpret because $T_{\mathbf o}$ is unknown in NPIV-O.
nodes.statement_short: Prior NPIV-O work stratifies on $O$ or assumes structure; an assumption of Chen et al. (2018) needed for their $L^2$ bound cannot hold in NPIV-O.
nodes.label: rem:partial_smoothing

nodes.name: Sieve ill-posedness with observed covariates (eq:chen_smoip_observed)
nodes.statement: \tau_J^{\mathrm{sieve}} \asymp \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf o\sim O}[\mu_{J, \mathbf o}^2]^{-\frac{1}{2}},
nodes.label: eq:chen_smoip_observed

nodes.name: Densities bounded above/below and smoothness orders m_o, m_z
nodes.statement: 1. The joint probability measures $P_{ZO}$ and $P_{XO}$ admit probability density functions $p_{ZO}$ and $p_{XO}$. There exists a universal constant $a>0$ such that $a^{-1} \geq p_{ZO}(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\geq a$ for all $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\in [0,1]^{d_z+d_o}$ and $a^{-1}\geq p_{XO}(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)$ for all $(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\in [0,1]^{d_x+d_o}$ and $p_{XO}(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\geq a$ for all $(\mathbf x,\mathbf o)\in [1/4,3/4]^{d_x+d_o}$. 2. \Cref{assn: technical} holds with the following $m_z, m_o \in \mathbb{N}^+$: \begin{talign} \begin{aligned} m_o := \left\lceil \frac{d_o}{2}\frac{1+2\left(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1\right) + \frac{d_o}{s_o}\left(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1\right)}{1 + 2\left(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1\right)} \right\rceil + 1, \quad m_z := \left\lceil \frac{d_z}{d_o}m_o\right\rceil . \end{aligned} \end{talign}
nodes.statement_short: $P_{ZO},P_{XO}$ have densities bounded above and below (on $[1/4,3/4]$ for $P_{XO}$), and the density-smoothness assumption holds with specific $m_o,m_z$.
nodes.label: ass:equiv_leb

nodes.name: Subgaussian residual
nodes.statement: For all $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\in \mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}$, the residual $\upsilon:= Y - (Tf_{\ast})(Z,O)$ is subgaussian conditioned on $Z=\mathbf z,O=\mathbf o$ with subgaussian norm at most $\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: The residual $\upsilon=Y-(Tf_*)(Z,O)$ is conditionally $\sigma$-subgaussian.
nodes.label: ass:subgaussian

nodes.name: Upper learning rate for KIV-O
nodes.statement: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assn: technical}, \ref{ass:equiv_leb} hold with parameters $m_z, m_o \in \mathbb{N}^{+}$, Assumption~\ref{ass:f_ast} holds with parameters $s_x, s_o > 0$, Assumptions~\ref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness}, \ref{ass:T_contractivity} hold with parameters $\eta_0, \eta_1$. We further suppose Assumptions~\ref{ass:T_injective} and \ref{ass:subgaussian} hold. We assume $t_o, t_z$ satisfy $2t_o \geq m_o > t_o > d_o/2$, $2 t_z \geq m_z > t_z > d_z/2$. We let \begin{align} \gamma_x = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{d_x}}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}, \quad \gamma_o = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}. \end{align} Define $m^{\dag} := (m_z t_z^{-1}) \wedge (m_o t_o^{-1})$ and $d^{\dag} := (d_z t_z^{-1}) \vee (d_o t_o^{-1})$. Let Stage I regularization parameter $\xi$ be given by $\tilde{n}^{-\frac{1}{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag} + \zeta}}$ for any $\zeta>0$; and Stage II regularization parameter $\lambda$ be given by $n^{-1}$. Suppose that $n\geq 1$ is sufficiently large, and $\tilde{n} \geq 1$ satisfies \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \tilde{n} \gtrsim n^{\frac{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag}/2 + \zeta}{m^{\dag}-1}} \vee n^{2 \frac{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag}/2 + \zeta}{m^{\dag}}}. \end{aligned} \end{align} Then with $P^{n+\tilde{n}}$-probability at least $1- 40e^{-\tau}$, we have \begin{align} \left\|\left[\hat{f}_{\lambda}\right] - f_{\ast}\right\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} \lesssim \tau n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1-\eta_0}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}} \cdot (\log n)^{\frac{d_x+d_o+1+d_x\eta_0}{2}} . \end{align}
assumptions: Suppose Assumptions~\ref{assn: technical}, \ref{ass:equiv_leb} hold with parameters $m_z, m_o \in \mathbb{N}^{+}$, Assumption~\ref{ass:f_ast} holds with parameters $s_x, s_o > 0$, Assumptions~\ref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness}, \ref{ass:T_contractivity} hold with parameters $\eta_0, \eta_1$. We further suppose Assumptions~\ref{ass:T_injective} and \ref{ass:subgaussian} hold. We assume $t_o, t_z$ satisfy $2t_o \geq m_o > t_o > d_o/2$, $2 t_z \geq m_z > t_z > d_z/2$. We let \begin{align} \gamma_x = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{d_x}}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}, \quad \gamma_o = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}. \end{align} Define $m^{\dag} := (m_z t_z^{-1}) \wedge (m_o t_o^{-1})$ and $d^{\dag} := (d_z t_z^{-1}) \vee (d_o t_o^{-1})$. Let Stage I regularization parameter $\xi$ be given by $\tilde{n}^{-\frac{1}{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag} + \zeta}}$ for any $\zeta>0$; and Stage II regularization parameter $\lambda$ be given by $n^{-1}$. Suppose that $n\geq 1$ is sufficiently large, and $\tilde{n} \geq 1$ satisfies \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \tilde{n} \gtrsim n^{\frac{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag}/2 + \zeta}{m^{\dag}-1}} \vee n^{2 \frac{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag}/2 + \zeta}{m^{\dag}}}. \end{aligned} \end{align}
conclusions: with $P^{n+\tilde{n}}$-probability at least $1- 40e^{-\tau}$, we have \begin{align} \left\|\left[\hat{f}_{\lambda}\right] - f_{\ast}\right\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} \lesssim \tau n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1-\eta_0}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}} \cdot (\log n)^{\frac{d_x+d_o+1+d_x\eta_0}{2}} . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: With lengthscales $\gamma_x,\gamma_o$ tuned to $n$, $\lambda=1/n$ and enough Stage I samples, KIV-O attains $L^2$ rate $n^{-(s_x/d_x+\eta_1-\eta_0)/(1+2(s_x/d_x+\eta_1)+(d_o/s_o)(s_x/d_x+\eta_1))}$ up to logs.
nodes.label: thm:upper_rate

nodes.name: Adaptive lengthscales gamma_x, gamma_o (eq:lengthscale_main)
nodes.statement: \gamma_x = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{d_x}}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}, \quad \gamma_o = n^{-\frac{\frac{1}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}}.
nodes.label: eq:lengthscale_main

nodes.name: Stage I sample size requirement (eq:m_sufficient_large)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \tilde{n} \gtrsim n^{\frac{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag}/2 + \zeta}{m^{\dag}-1}} \vee n^{2 \frac{m^{\dag} + d^{\dag}/2 + \zeta}{m^{\dag}}}. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:m_sufficient_large

nodes.name: Upper rate (eq:upper_rate)
nodes.statement: \left\|\left[\hat{f}_{\lambda}\right] - f_{\ast}\right\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} \lesssim \tau n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1-\eta_0}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}} \cdot (\log n)^{\frac{d_x+d_o+1+d_x\eta_0}{2}} .
nodes.label: eq:upper_rate

nodes.name: Regime of large Stage I sample size
nodes.statement: In \Cref{thm:upper_rate}, we present the regime where the Stage I sample size $\tilde{n}$ is sufficiently large relative to the Stage II sample size (see Eq.~\eqref{eq:m_sufficient_large}). This is the appropriate regime where we can study rate-optimality because we present a minimax lower bound in \Cref{thm:lower_rate} with respect to the class of estimators that only utilize Stage II samples. It is nevertheless possible to derive upper bounds with respect to both $n$ and $\tilde{n}$ without restrictions on the relative size of $n, \tilde{n}$. It remains a challenging open problem, however, to establish rate optimality for estimators utilizing a split dataset of the form $\{(\tilde{\mathbf z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf o}_i, \tilde{\mathbf x}_i)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}}$ and $\{(\mathbf z_i, \mathbf o_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$, even for the standard NPIV setting \citep{chen2011rate, Chen_2018, meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel}.
nodes.label: rem: stage_1_lower_bound

nodes.name: Rate optimality with split samples
nodes.statement: It remains a challenging open problem, however, to establish rate optimality for estimators utilizing a split dataset of the form $\{(\tilde{\mathbf z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf o}_i, \tilde{\mathbf x}_i)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}}$ and $\{(\mathbf z_i, \mathbf o_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}$, even for the standard NPIV setting \citep{chen2011rate, Chen_2018, meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel}.
nodes.statement_short: Open: rate optimality for estimators that use split Stage I/Stage II samples, even in standard NPIV.

nodes.name: Upper rate interpolates between NPIV and nonparametric regression
nodes.statement: Our derived upper rate interpolates between the known optimal $L^2$-rates for NPIV without observed covariates and anisotropic kernel ridge regression. \\ 1. When $\eta_0 = \eta_1 = 0$ and $X=Z$, i.e. $T$ is the identity mapping, our setting reduces to nonparametric regression where the target function lies in the anisotropic Besov space $B_{2, \infty}^{s_x, s_o}(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O})$. The upper rate simplifies to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_P(n^{-\frac{1}{2\tilde{s}+1}})$ with $\tilde{s} = (d_o/s_o + d_x/s_x)^{-1}$ being the intrinsic smoothness, which matches the known optimal learning rate of regression with an anisotropic Besov target function~\citep{hoffman2002random,hang2021optimal}. \\ 2. When $d_o = 0$, our setting reduces to NPIV without observed covariates where the target function $f_\ast$ lies in an isotropic Besov space $B_{2, \infty}^{s_x}(\mathcal{X})$. We take $\eta_1 = \eta_0 = \eta$ following \citet{Chen_2018, chen2011rate} which employs a single parameter to characterize both the ill-posedness and contractivity, then our upper learning rate simplifies to $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_P(n^{-\frac{s_x}{d_x+2(s_x+\eta d_x)}})$, which matches the known optimal rate in NPIV regression~\citep[Corollary 3.1]{Chen_2018}.
nodes.statement_short: For $T=$ id the rate recovers the optimal anisotropic Besov regression rate; for $d_o=0$ it recovers the optimal NPIV rate.
nodes.label: rem:interpolate

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement:
The proof of \Cref{thm:upper_rate} is given in \Cref{sec:proof_upper} in the Supplement. Here we give an outline of our proof to facilitate a deeper understanding of both the assumptions and the results. Define $\bar{f}_{\lambda}$ as the oracle estimator for Stage II with access to the true conditional mean embedding $F_\ast$ and recall $\hat{f}_{\lambda}$ for comparison:
\begin{align}
    \bar{f}_{\lambda} &:= \underset{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}{\arg\min} \lambda \|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}( y_i - \langle f, F_\ast(\mathbf z_i,\mathbf o_i) \otimes \phi_{O, \gamma_o}(\mathbf o_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} )^2 . \\
    \hat{f}_{\lambda} &:= \underset{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}{\arg\min} \lambda \|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}( y_i - \langle f, \hat{F}_{\xi}(\mathbf z_i,\mathbf o_i) \otimes \phi_{O, \gamma_o}(\mathbf o_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} )^2 .
\end{align}
The proof can be summarized in 3 steps.
We upper bound $\|T[\hat{f}_\lambda]-T[\bar{f}_\lambda]\|_{L^2\left(P_{Z O}\right)}$ in \textit{Step 1} and upper bound $\|T[\bar{f}_\lambda]-T f_*\|_{L^2(P_{Z O})}$ in \textit{Step 2}, which induce an upper bound on $\|T[\hat{f}_\lambda]-T f_*\|_{L^2(P_{Z O})}$ via a triangular inequality. In \textit{Step 3}, we apply the partial measure of ill-posedness to obtain an upper bound on $\|[\hat{f}_\lambda]- f_*\|_{L^2(P_{XO})}$. 
We highlight our technical contributions in each step with \Cref{rem:tensor_krr} and \Cref{rem:no_clipping}.

\textit{Step 1} We upper bound $\|T[\hat{f}_\lambda]-T[\bar{f}_\lambda]\|_{L^2\left(P_{Z O}\right)}$. By their definition in Eq.~\eqref{eq:hat_f_lambda_main} and Eq.~\eqref{eq:bar_f_lambda_main}, the discrepancy between $\hat{f}_\lambda$ and $\bar{f}_\lambda$ arises solely from the difference between $\hat{F}_{\xi}$ and $F_\ast$; hence it corresponds to Stage I error. First, we prove in \Cref{prop:T_hat_f_bar_f} that $\|T[\hat{f}_\lambda]-T[\bar{f}_\lambda]\|_{L^2\left(P_{Z O}\right)}$ can be upper bounded by an expression involving $\|\hat{F}_{\xi}-F_*\|_{\mathcal{G}}$ and $\|F_*-\hat{F}_{\xi}\|_{L^2(\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{O}; \mathcal{H}_{X,\gamma_x})}$, where we recall that $\mathcal{G}$ denotes the unique vector-valued RKHS induced by
the operator-valued kernel $K$ defined in Eq. \eqref{eq:op_val_kernel}. 
To obtain high-probability upper bounds on both of these quantities, we adapt the existing optimal learning rates on CME from \citet{lietal2022optimal} to our setting with a tensor product RKHS. 
The fact that we require upper learning rate for $\|F_*-\hat{F}_{\xi}\|_{\mathcal{G}}$ imposes the conditions $m_o>t_o$ and $m_z>t_z$, so the CME $F_\ast$ lies in a smoother space than RKHS $\mathcal{G}$. Specifically, $F_{\ast}$ belongs to the \emph{power space} $[\mathcal{G}]^{m^{\dag}}$ (See Eq.~\eqref{eq:F_ast_power_space}).
In addition, the constraints $2 t_o>m_o$ and $2 t_z>m_z$ reflect the saturation effect inherent in Tikhonov regularization~\citep{bauer2007regularization, lu2024saturation, meunier2024optimalratesvectorvaluedspectral}. 
These constraints can be removed to allow for greater smoothness of $F_\ast$ by employing spectral regularization~\citep{meunier2024optimalratesvectorvaluedspectral}. 
The appearance of an arbitrarily small $\zeta>0$ in Stage I regularization parameter $\xi$ reflects the fact that, after reordering, the eigenvalues of the tensor product operator exhibit slower decay than those of the individual components, owing to an extra logarithmic term~\citep{krieg2018tensor}.

\begin{rem}[Tensor product kernel ridge regression] In the above step, we generalize the upper learning rate for vector-valued kernel ridge regression to the setting of tensor product kernels (See \Cref{prop:cme_rate}). Although tensor product kernels have been widely used in kernel-based hypothesis tests~\citep{gretton2007kernel,GreGyo10,SejGreBer13,gretton2015characteristic,ZhaFilGreSej18,AlbLaurMarMey22,szabo2018characteristic},  kernel independent component analysis \citep{BacJor02,SheJegGre09},  and feature selection \citep{SonSmoGreBedetal12,LiPogSutGre21}, they have  been less well studied  in kernel ridge regression, with the exception of \citet{hang2021optimal} for Gaussian kernels. Our analysis is also applicable to real-valued kernel ridge regression with tensor product kernels.
\end{rem}
\textit{Step 2} We upper bound $\|T[\bar{f}_\lambda]-T f_*\|_{L^2(P_{Z O})}$. We follow the approach in \citet{blanchard2018optimal, meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel}, where it is observed (in the standard NPIV case) that this term corresponds to the learning risk of a kernel ridge regression problem with an appropriately defined RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{FO} \subseteq \{\mathcal{Z}\times \mathcal{O}\to \mathbb{R}\}$, namely the RKHS induced by the feature map $(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\mapsto F_{\ast}(\mathbf z,\mathbf o)\otimes \phi_{O,2}(\mathbf o)$. We refer the reader to \Cref{sec:defi_H_FO} in the Supplement for the definition of $\mathcal{H}_{FO}$. Our construction is adapted from \citet[Appendix E.1.2]{meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel}. However, unlike \citet{blanchard2018optimal, meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel} who only consider fixed RKHSs, we employ tensor product Gaussian RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x, \gamma_o}$ with \emph{adaptive} length-scales $\gamma_x, \gamma_o$ (as in Eq.~\eqref{eq:lengthscale_main}) to capture the anisotropic smoothness of $f_\ast \in B^{s_x, s_o}_{2,\infty}(\mathcal{X}\times \mathcal{O})$~\citep{hang2021optimal}. 
When $\eta_1 = 0$, our choice of length-scales $\gamma_x, \gamma_o$ coincides with that of kernel ridge regression in \citet{hang2021optimal}. 
The logarithmic factor \smash{$(\log n)^{\frac{d_x+d_o+1}{2}}$} in Eq.~\eqref{eq:upper_rate} arises from the entropy numbers of the Gaussian RKHS in this step (see \Cref{sec:capacity} in the Supplement and \citet[Proposition 1]{hang2021optimal}). 
\begin{rem}[Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space target functions] To establish learning rates for kernel ridge regression, there are two main techniques in the literature: the empirical process technique~\citep{steinwart2008support,steinwart2009optimal} and the integral operator technique~\citep{fischer2020sobolev,Lin_2020,smale2007learning,caponnetto2007optimal,blanchard2018optimal}. Previous works on Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space targets~\citep{eberts2013optimal, hang2021optimal,hamm2021adaptive}  rely on an oracle inequality proved via empirical process techniques~\citep[Theorem 7.23]{steinwart2008support}, which necessitates a clipping operation on the estimator. 
    On the other hand, the integral operator technique avoids the clipping operation, but it requires the target $f_\ast$ in a power space of the RKHS---a condition known as the source condition~\citep[SRC]{fischer2020sobolev}---which does not hold for Besov space targets and Gaussian RKHSs. 

    In our proof in step 2, we prove an upper learning rate of Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space target functions \emph{without} clipping the estimator.
    Specifically, we combine the two techniques above, in that we bound the approximation error with \citet{hang2021optimal}, while we bound the estimation error with the integral operator technique~\citep{fischer2020sobolev}.
    To be precise, define 
    \begin{align} f_{\lambda} := arg\,min_{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}\lambda\|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \|T([f] - f_{\ast})\|^2_{L^2(P_{ZO})}. 
    \end{align}
    The learning risk $ \|T([\bar{f}_{\lambda}] - f_\ast) \|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ can be decomposed into an estimation error term $\|T([\bar{f}_{\lambda}] - [f_{\lambda}])\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ and an approximation error term $\|T([f_{\lambda}] - f_{\ast})\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$. 
    We upper bound the estimation error with \citet[Theorem 16]{fischer2020sobolev}, once we prove that the RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{FO}$ satisfies an \emph{embedding property} (see \citet[EMB]{fischer2020sobolev}), which avoids the clipping operation.
    We upper bound the approximation error with \citet[Theorem 4]{hang2021optimal}, which avoids the source condition. 
\end{rem}


\textit{Step 3} We combine the above two terms $\|T[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - T[\bar{f}_{\lambda}]\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ and $\|T[\bar{f}_{\lambda}] - Tf_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ through a triangle inequality, which gives an upper bound on the projected risk $\|T[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - Tf_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$.
\vspace{-10pt}
\begin{align} \|T[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - Tf_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})} \lesssim (\log n)^{\frac{d_x+d_o+1}{2}} n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}} .
\end{align}
To bound the unprojected risk $\|[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - f_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$, it seems all that remains is to apply the Fourier measure of partial ill-posedness in \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} to remove $T$. 
Unfortunately, however, \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} only holds for functions in $\mathrm{LF}(\gamma)$ (Eq.~\eqref{eq:HF_LF}) with low partial Fourier frequency in $\mathcal{X}$. Notice that for a function $f \in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$, its partial Fourier spectrum $|\mathcal{F}[f(\cdot,\mathbf o)](\boldsymbol{\omega}_x)|$ decays exponentially fast as $\|\boldsymbol{\omega}_x\|_2\to\infty$~\citep[Theorem 10.12]{wendland2004scattered}
\begin{talign} (\forall\mathbf o\in \mathcal{O}), \quad\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d_x}}|\mathcal{F}[f(\cdot,\mathbf o)](\boldsymbol{\omega}_x)|^2\exp\left(\frac{1}{4} \gamma_x^2\|\boldsymbol{\omega}_x\|^2_{2} \right) \;\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\omega}_x < \infty .
\end{talign}
This exponential decay implies that $\hat{f}_\lambda(\cdot, \mathbf o)$ satisfies the conditions of \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness} up to some logarithmic factors as reflected by \smash{$(\log n)^{\frac{d_x\eta_0}{2}}$} in Eq.~\eqref{eq:upper_rate}.
For $f_{\ast}$, we find an auxiliary function $f_{\mathrm{aux}}\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$ that is close to $f_{\ast}$ in $L^2(P_{XO})$-norm and agrees with $f_{\ast}$ at low frequencies. To be precise, we require that $\mathrm{supp}(\mathcal{F}[(f_{\mathrm{aux}} - f_{\ast})(\cdot,\mathbf o)]) \subseteq \{\boldsymbol{\omega}_x:\|\boldsymbol{\omega}_x\|_
{2} \geq \gamma_x^{-1} \}$ for any $\mathbf o\in \mathcal{O}$, and we refer the reader to Eq.~\eqref{eq:f_aux} for the exact definition of $f_{\mathrm{aux}}$. Hence, 
\begin{talign*}
    \|[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - f_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} 
    \lesssim \|[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - f_{\mathrm{aux}} \|_{L^2(P_{XO})} 
    \lesssim \gamma_x^{-\eta_0d_x}(\log n)^{\frac{d_x\eta_0}{2}} \|T[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - T f_{\mathrm{aux}} \|_{L^2(P_{ZO})} .
\end{talign*}
In the last step, we utilize the Fourier measure of partial ill-posedness in \Cref{ass:T_frequency_ill_posedness}, and the fact that $\hat{f}_{\lambda}, f_{\mathrm{aux}} \in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}$.
The above equation is a sketch where formal derivations can be found at the beginning of \Cref{sec:proof_upper}, particularly Eq. \eqref{eq:eq_to_refer_main_pf_sketch} and Eq. \eqref{eq:eq_to_refer_main_pf_sketch_final}. 
Combining the above relation and the choice of $\gamma_x$ in Eq.~\eqref{eq:lengthscale_main} concludes the proof of \Cref{thm:upper_rate}.
nodes.statement_short: Three-step sketch: bound the Stage I and Stage II projected errors, combine by the triangle inequality, then remove $T$ via partial ill-posedness using an auxiliary low-frequency function $f_{aux}$.

nodes.name: Oracle Stage II estimator bar f_lambda (eq:bar_f_lambda_main)
nodes.statement: \bar{f}_{\lambda} &:= \underset{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}{\arg\min} \lambda \|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}( y_i - \langle f, F_\ast(\mathbf z_i,\mathbf o_i) \otimes \phi_{O, \gamma_o}(\mathbf o_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} )^2 .
nodes.label: eq:bar_f_lambda_main

nodes.name: KIV-O Stage II estimator hat f_lambda (eq:hat_f_lambda_main)
nodes.statement: \hat{f}_{\lambda} &:= \underset{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}{\arg\min} \lambda \|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \frac{1}{n}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}( y_i - \langle f, \hat{F}_{\xi}(\mathbf z_i,\mathbf o_i) \otimes \phi_{O, \gamma_o}(\mathbf o_i) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} )^2 .
nodes.label: eq:hat_f_lambda_main

nodes.name: Tensor product kernel ridge regression
nodes.statement: In the above step, we generalize the upper learning rate for vector-valued kernel ridge regression to the setting of tensor product kernels (See \Cref{prop:cme_rate}). Although tensor product kernels have been widely used in kernel-based hypothesis tests~\citep{gretton2007kernel,GreGyo10,SejGreBer13,gretton2015characteristic,ZhaFilGreSej18,AlbLaurMarMey22,szabo2018characteristic}, kernel independent component analysis \citep{BacJor02,SheJegGre09}, and feature selection \citep{SonSmoGreBedetal12,LiPogSutGre21}, they have been less well studied in kernel ridge regression, with the exception of \citet{hang2021optimal} for Gaussian kernels. Our analysis is also applicable to real-valued kernel ridge regression with tensor product kernels.
nodes.label: rem:tensor_krr

nodes.name: Gaussian KRR with Besov targets without clipping
nodes.statement: To establish learning rates for kernel ridge regression, there are two main techniques in the literature: the empirical process technique~\citep{steinwart2008support,steinwart2009optimal} and the integral operator technique~\citep{fischer2020sobolev,Lin_2020,smale2007learning,caponnetto2007optimal,blanchard2018optimal}. Previous works on Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space targets~\citep{eberts2013optimal, hang2021optimal,hamm2021adaptive} rely on an oracle inequality proved via empirical process techniques~\citep[Theorem 7.23]{steinwart2008support}, which necessitates a clipping operation on the estimator. On the other hand, the integral operator technique avoids the clipping operation, but it requires the target $f_\ast$ in a power space of the RKHS---a condition known as the source condition~\citep[SRC]{fischer2020sobolev}---which does not hold for Besov space targets and Gaussian RKHSs. In our proof in step 2, we prove an upper learning rate of Gaussian kernel ridge regression with Besov space target functions \emph{without} clipping the estimator. Specifically, we combine the two techniques above, in that we bound the approximation error with \citet{hang2021optimal}, while we bound the estimation error with the integral operator technique~\citep{fischer2020sobolev}. To be precise, define \begin{align} f_{\lambda} := arg\,min_{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}\lambda\|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \|T([f] - f_{\ast})\|^2_{L^2(P_{ZO})}. \end{align} The learning risk $ \|T([\bar{f}_{\lambda}] - f_\ast) \|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ can be decomposed into an estimation error term $\|T([\bar{f}_{\lambda}] - [f_{\lambda}])\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$ and an approximation error term $\|T([f_{\lambda}] - f_{\ast})\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})}$. We upper bound the estimation error with \citet[Theorem 16]{fischer2020sobolev}, once we prove that the RKHS $\mathcal{H}_{FO}$ satisfies an \emph{embedding property} (see \citet[EMB]{fischer2020sobolev}), which avoids the clipping operation. We upper bound the approximation error with \citet[Theorem 4]{hang2021optimal}, which avoids the source condition.
nodes.statement_short: Combines empirical-process approximation bounds (Hang & Steinwart) with integral-operator estimation bounds (Fischer & Steinwart) to avoid clipping the estimator.
nodes.label: rem:no_clipping

nodes.name: Population regularized solution f_lambda (eq:f_lambda_main)
nodes.statement: f_{\lambda} := arg\,min_{f\in \mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}}\lambda\|f\|^2_{\mathcal{H}_{\gamma_x,\gamma_o}} + \|T([f] - f_{\ast})\|^2_{L^2(P_{ZO})}.
nodes.label: eq:f_lambda_main

nodes.name: Projected risk bound (eq:projected_risk_main)
nodes.statement: \|T[\hat{f}_{\lambda}] - Tf_{\ast}\|_{L^2(P_{ZO})} \lesssim (\log n)^{\frac{d_x+d_o+1}{2}} n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)}} .
nodes.label: eq:projected_risk_main

nodes.name: Extension to more anisotropy
nodes.statement: For simplicity of presentation, we focus on the case where anisotropic smoothness exists across $(X,O)$ but we assume no anisotropy within $X$ and $O$. The KIV-O algorithm with adaptive length-scales and its associated learning rate can both be easily extended to the fully anisotropic setting, where $f_\ast \in B_{2, \infty}^{\boldsymbol{s}} (\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{O})$ with $\boldsymbol{s}=[s_1, \ldots, s_{d_x}, s_{d_x+1}, \ldots, s_{d_x+d_o}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x+d_o}$, a generalization of previous results from anisotropic nonparametric regression~\citep{hang2021optimal, suzuki2021deep,hoffman2002random} to anisotropic NPIV-O. This is particularly relevant in applied work, where the observed covariates $O$ are often of high dimensionality, because practitioners tend to adjust for as many observed covariates as possible to mitigate unobserved confounding. In such cases, our KIV-O algorithm with adaptive length-scales adapts to the intrinsic smoothness with respect to $O$. This mitigates the slow rates typically caused by a high ambient dimension when the intrinsic smoothness is high, as our learning rates avoid being limited by the worst-case smoothness across all dimensions.
nodes.label: rem:extension_anisotropy

nodes.name: Admissible distribution
nodes.statement_short: A distribution of $(Z,X,O,Y)$ is admissible if it satisfies the density, completeness, boundedness and subgaussian assumptions, with $f_*$ Besov and $T$ partially contractive.

nodes.name: Samples D, D_1, D_2
nodes.statement: For an \emph{admissible} distribution $P_{ZXOY}$, consider $\mathcal{D} = (\mathbf z_i, \mathbf x_i, \mathbf o_i, y_i)_{i=1}^N, N \geq 1$ sampled i.i.d from $P_{ZXOY}$ and consider $\mathcal{D}_1 = (\tilde{\mathbf z}_i, \tilde{\mathbf o}_i, \tilde{\mathbf x}_i)_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}}$ and $\mathcal{D}_2 = (\mathbf z_i, \mathbf o_i, y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $\tilde{n},n \leq N$.

nodes.name: Minimax lower bound for NPIV-O
nodes.statement: There exists an \emph{admissible} distribution $P_{ZXOY}$ such that for all learning methods $(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2) \mapsto \hat{f}_{(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2)}$, for all $\tau>0$, and sufficiently large $n\geq 1$, the following minimax lower bound holds with $P^{n}$-probability at least $1- C_1 \tau^2$ and $P^{\tilde{n}}$-almost surely , \begin{align} \left\| \hat{f}_{(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2)} - f_\ast \right\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} \geq C_0 \tau^2 n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}\frac{s_x}{d_x}}} (\log n)^{-2s_x - d_x} . \end{align}
assumptions: There exists an \emph{admissible} distribution $P_{ZXOY}$ such that for all learning methods $(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2) \mapsto \hat{f}_{(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2)}$, for all $\tau>0$, and sufficiently large $n\geq 1$
conclusions: the following minimax lower bound holds with $P^{n}$-probability at least $1- C_1 \tau^2$ and $P^{\tilde{n}}$-almost surely , \begin{align} \left\| \hat{f}_{(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2)} - f_\ast \right\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} \geq C_0 \tau^2 n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}\frac{s_x}{d_x}}} (\log n)^{-2s_x - d_x} . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Some admissible distribution forces every estimator to have $L^2$ error at least $n^{-(s_x/d_x)/(1+2(s_x/d_x+\eta_1)+(d_o/s_o)(s_x/d_x))}$ up to logs.
nodes.label: thm:lower_rate

nodes.name: Minimax lower rate (eq:minimax_lower_rate)
nodes.statement: \left\| \hat{f}_{(\mathcal{D}_1,\mathcal{D}_2)} - f_\ast \right\|_{L^2(P_{XO})} \geq C_0 \tau^2 n^{-\frac{\frac{s_x}{d_x}}{1+2(\frac{s_x}{d_x}+\eta_1)+\frac{d_o}{s_o}\frac{s_x}{d_x}}} (\log n)^{-2s_x - d_x} .
nodes.label: eq:minimax_lower_rate

nodes.name: Gap between upper and lower bounds
nodes.statement: There remains a gap between the upper and minimax lower bounds even if we take $\eta_1 = \eta_0$ and ignore the logarithmic terms.
assumptions: even if we take $\eta_1 = \eta_0$ and ignore the logarithmic terms
conclusions: There remains a gap between the upper and minimax lower bounds

nodes.name: Lower rate interpolates between NPIV and nonparametric regression
nodes.statement: Similar to the \Cref{rem:interpolate} of the upper learning rate, our minimax lower learning rate also interpolates between the known optimal $L^2$-rates for NPIV without observed covariates ($d_o = 0$) and anisotropic non-parametric regression ($\eta_1 = \eta_0 = 0$).
nodes.label: rem:lb_main_rem

nodes.name: Comparison to existing L2-minimax lower bounds for NPIV
nodes.statement: The work \citet{chen2011rate} established minimax rate-optimality in $L^2$-norm for NPIV under an \emph{approximation condition} and \emph{link condition}. For a conveniently chosen compact operator $B$, the approximation condition characterizes the smoothness of the structural function by the optimal $L^2$-rate approximation by the eigenvectors of $B$, and the link condition relates the mapping properties of the conditional expectation operator $T$ to the Hilbert scale generated by $B$. This framework subsumes an earlier minimax convergence rate result in \citet{HallHorowitz2005}, and was subsequently instantiated in \citet{Chen_2018} for a $B$ constructed via a wavelet basis, and generalized to kernel instrumental variables in \citet{meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel} with a Hilbert scale given by the covariance operator of the RKHS. A crucial limitation of this framework is the link condition can only hold if the singular values of the conditional expectation operator are decaying to zero. Thus the minimax framework given by the link condition is applicable only when $T$ is compact, and is not suitable for our observed covariates setting.

nodes.name: Proof outline of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement:
We give an outline of our proof for \Cref{thm:lower_rate} to facilitate a deeper
understanding of both the assumptions and the results. The full proof is in \Cref{sec:NPIR_lower_appendix} in the Supplementary. The primary strategy in deriving minimax lower bounds is to construct a family of distributions that are similar enough so that they are statistically indistinguishable, but for which the target function of interest is maximally separated. 
This implies no estimator can have error uniformly smaller than this separation. 

Following prior work in the literature~\citep{chen2011rate,meunier2024nonparametricinstrumentalregressionkernel}, we observe that NPIV-O in Eq.~\eqref{eq:npiv_o_intro} is statistically more challenging than the reduced form non-parametric indirect regression with observed covariates (NPIR-O) with a \emph{known} operator $T:L^2(P_{XO})\to L^2(P_{ZO})$. The NPIR-O model is defined below
\begin{align} Y= (Tf_*)(Z, O) + \upsilon,
\end{align}
where $\upsilon$ is a random variable such that $\mathbb{E}[\upsilon\mid Z,O] = 0$, and it satisfies \Cref{ass:subgaussian}, and where $T$ satisfies \Cref{ass:T_injective}, \Cref{ass:T_contractivity} and the associated conditional distribution $P_{X\mid Z,O}$ satisfies \Cref{assn: technical}. We refer the reader to \Cref{sec:npir_reduction} in the Supplementary Material for a detailed definition of the NPIR-O model class. We formally prove in \Cref{lem:npir_o_more_informative} in the Supplementary that it suffices to construct a minimax lower bound for the NPIR-O model. 
To this end, we adapt Theorem 20 of \cite{fischer2020sobolev}, which is itself an adaptation of Proposition 2.3 of \citet{Tsybakov}.
